transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-03 14:00 PT / 21:00Z
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Luca Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jon Vega (Redwood CSM), Eli Morris (BrightCart CTO), Sara Nguyen (BrightCart ML Lead), Ravi Patel (BrightCart Platform), Nora Feldman (BrightCart Product)

Summary (auto): quick hosted API walkthrough focused on streaming behavior, client-side retry strategies, timeouts and idempotency. Customer is evaluating hosted first, then Dedicated if latency predictability becomes necessary.

[00:00] Maya: hey everybody thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:06] Eli: yes, loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:08] Luca: hi team — Luca from Redwood, i'll be doing most of the demo bits, you might see me screenshare.
[00:12] Sara: great, we are mostly interested in how streaming behaves for our chat widget and how to handle partial responses and retries, plus how billing works for partial tokens.

[00:25] Luca: perfect, quick agenda: 1) hosted API quickstart and console tour, 2) streaming response behavior and partial tokens, 3) retry/backoff and idempotency keys, 4) timeout strategies and client-side recommendations, 5) q&a and next steps.
[00:40] Ravi: just one ask — we have strict SLOs on 95th percentile latency, and we may run a 10k concurrent user load in peak; curious how hosted handles bursty spikes.

[01:02] Luca: good question — hosted has autoscaling and we also suggest pinning model variants and using fallback model policy; but for hard 95th SLOs Dedicated is usually the long-term solution. For hosted we recommend a combination of prefix caching, aggressive client-side retry shaping, and short timeouts to fall back quickly.
[01:28] [screen share starts] Luca: here is the console quickstart — you can see the model catalog, run playground requests. we'll flip to the streams example.

[01:45] Luca: when you call the chat endpoint with stream=true you get incremental events. typical patterns are SSE or websockets; the SDK wraps that. important to note — the server will bill tokens as they are emitted, so if you time out mid-stream you still pay for tokens delivered.
[02:15] Nora: can you clarify — if the client times out after receiving two chunks, do we get billed for the in-flight tokens?
[02:20] Lucas [sic]: yes, charged for tokens generated up to the point of termination. Minor transcription note: speaker label mis-attributed here.
[02:30] Luca: also there are partial tokens and then final delimiting event; costs reflect generation not delivery.

[02:50] Sara: for the UI we plan to render partial partials as they arrive; any recommendations for deduping partial updates?
[02:56] Luca: keep a buffer and commit on delimiter or on silence threshold, and idempotency keys help if you need safe retries — though idempotency on streaming is trickier because it's incremental. Usually we recommend checkpointing at message boundaries: include a client_message_id and an idempotency header for each user turn.

[03:25] Eli: what's the right header format? do you have an example?
[03:28] Luca: yes — example: X-Idempotency-Key: <uuid:user-turn> plus X-Request-Metadata: {conversation_id, turn_index}. For retry-safe completes you should retry only the final completion call with the same key. We'll share snippets.

[03:50] Priya: when you say final completion call — do you mean non-streaming completion?
[03:54] Luca: right — either you switch to a non-streaming call for the last chunk or you rely on server-side dedupe using the idempotency key. Hosted supports idempotency for write-like calls and completes, but streaming intermediate partials are best treated as best-effort.

[04:22] [05:00] Luca: moving on to retries — typical pattern is client-side exponential backoff with jitter for transient errors (5xx, 429). For safety use an overall operation timeout (for example 10s for a quick chat response) and a shorter streaming chunk timeout (2–3s). If you get a 429 we recommend backoff respecting Retry-After header when present.
[05:40] Sara: is there any per-route rate-limit info in the response so we can adapt?
[05:44] Luca: yes we return standard rate-limit headers and a quota status in the dashboard; plus the console shows per-route usage. We'll also show the Optimize tab with batching suggestions.

[06:05] Luca: quick demo of a client retry loop in node — code snippet: start request with idempotency key, listen for stream events, on transient failure check status code; if non-terminal (e.g., connection reset) re-establish using same key for finalization. for full restarts you may need to reconstruct the last user message.
[06:31] Ravi: can you show a sample policy for reconnects vs restart?
[06:35] Luca: sure — policy we recommend: 1) on network glitch reconnect up to 2 times with linear backoff, re-use same client turn key; 2) if reconnect fails escalate to non-streaming completion with same key; 3) if non-streaming also fails mark turn for server-side retry by backend job so user isn't blocked. We'll attach this flowchart.

[07:10] [07:40] Luca: note on idempotency uniqueness: include user id + conversation id + turn sequence in the uuid, avoid pure timestamps. avoid reusing keys across different logical turns.

[07:55] Eli: what about timeouts — if we set a short client timeout we reduce p50/p95 but may increase failed turns — tradeoff?
[08:02] Maya: exactly, it's a tradeoff between perceived latency and completion reliability. For storefront chat we often use an optimistic timeout of 3.5–4s and then fetch a final non-streaming completion in the background for exactness; show the quick fallback pattern.
[08:30] Sara: this background final completion — won't the user get duplicate content?
[08:33] Luca: you indicate the UI to prefer streamed content then patch if final completion differs, or you use rerank/post-process to merge. Use client_message_id to detect duplicates and only patch if there is a meaningful delta.

[09:00] [09:12] Priya: how do we monitor partial token costs — any console metrics?
[09:16] Luca: console shows per-request token breakdown, streaming tokens are attributed as they are generated. Optimize module will suggest batching or prefix-caching patterns if we detect repeated prefixes. We'll show an example where caching reduced token usage by 23% for a FAQ bot.
[09:45] [10:00] Luca: quick note on batching — if you have many concurrent short requests consider request multiplexing at your gateway. Redwood's batching controls let you trade off latency for cost; Optimize will suggest quantization or smaller model variants for lower cost.

[10:30] Nora: security / data retention — we need to keep logs for 90 days and can't send PII outside region. How does hosted handle region and KMS?
[10:40] Maya: hosted currently supports region selection and we have KMS integration for encryption at rest; for strict data residency Dedicated or Private offering is recommended. We'll send security pack and SOC2 docs.

[11:05] [11:40] Luca: back to retries — show demo of a stream being interrupted, client reconnect and finalization with idempotency key in dev console. [screen action] you can see the partial events showing chunk1, chunk2 then reconnect. On reconnect the server emits a resume token if available. If server-side resume isn't possible client must re-request the missing final chunk.
[12:20] Sara: what about resume semantics — do you send the last token index?
[12:24] Luca: yes we include a resume cursor in the final event; but it's best-effort between servers, not guaranteed across model variant fallback. If fallback occurred resume may not be possible so fall back to re-request.

[12:50] Eli: any instrumentation or traces to correlate user request to server trace?
[12:53] Priya: we can add request-id headers and the console has per-request traces and token timeline. We'll show a sample trace later.

[13:20] Luca: briefly on error classification: 4xx usually indicates an input or auth issue; 429 is throttling; 5xx likely a transient service error. For 5xx we retry with exponential backoff. For streaming we also detect truncated events and treat as transient for a short window.

[14:05] [14:30] Luca: demo: sending a message with temperature 0.2 and max_tokens 128, stream=true. you see tokens coming in; if you increase temperature you get more varied outputs but also potentially longer generations. For UI we suggest controlling max_tokens tightly for predictable latency.
[15:10] Sara: do you have adaptive param recommendations per center?
[15:14] Luca: yes — console Optimize will recommend param presets per workload — e.g., conversational FAQ vs creative summaries. We'll share a csv of presets.

[15:40] Luca: another tip — use stop sequences and token limits to bound cost. If you have known templates, use prefix caching to avoid re-sending the same system prompt every time. That reduces tokens and latency.

[16:03] Ravi: curious about SDKs: do they expose reconnect helpers and idempotency helpers?
[16:08] Luca: yes the official SDKs include a RetryHelper and StreamingClient that handle reconnects, backoff, and can attach idempotency keys automatically if you provide a conversation id. We'll share code links.

[16:40] Maya: quick pricing note — hosted charges per token for generations and embeddings separately; partial streamed tokens are billed. For pilot we can offer reserved capacity discounts if usage stabilizes.

[17:05] Nora: we might start with hosted for a 3-month pilot and move to Dedicated if p95 can't be met.
[17:10] Maya: that's a common path — start hosted, iterate, then transition to Dedicated with predictable commit if you need the 95th percentile hitting consistently.

[17:35] [18:00] Q&A:
[18:05] Eli: are there tools to measure effective latency for UI?
[18:09] Priya: console traces and synthetic canaries can measure time-to-first-byte and time-to-complete; we also expose token-level timing.
[18:24] Sara: how do we test large concurrent loads for hosted?
[18:28] Luca: we can run a joint benchmark; SEs run a small perf test against your sample traffic profile — that was one of the next steps.

[19:00] Maya: ok recap — we'll send pilot pricing and SLA, SE to share retry/playbook and idempotency snippets, customer to upload traffic histogram. We also promised security docs.
[19:20] Eli: thanks all — this was helpful. we'll sync internally and aim to get the histogram over by Friday.

[19:32] [19:40] Maya: great thanks everyone. end call.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker labels occasionally generic; some product names or acronyms mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cache -> K-V cash), small hesitations removed.
